name: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis

possible: Enterococcus species (more relevant in healthcare-associated SBP or prior antibiotic exposure)
pathogens.why: SBP is monomicrobial in the great majority of cases and reflects bacterial translocation from the gut, dominated by gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae, with gram-positive cocci accounting for most of the remainder.

investigations.test: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture
investigations.why: Defines the diagnosis (neutrophil count ≥250/mm³) and identifies the organism for targeted therapy — essential before committing to a full antibiotic course where feasible.
Frequently positive and may identify the organism even when ascitic fluid culture is negative (culture-negative neutrocytic ascites).
Guides decision on adjunctive albumin and assesses for hepatorenal syndrome, a major complication of SBP.

investigations.test: Liver function tests and coagulation profile
investigations.why: Establishes baseline severity of underlying liver disease, relevant to prognosis and overall management.

reason: altered sensorium (which can be the sole presenting feature of SBP, especially in those with underlying hepatic encephalopathy)

raises concern for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis should be performed promptly, and empiric antibiotics should be started once ascitic fluid neutrophil count supports the diagnosis (or immediately if paracentesis is delayed and suspicion is high), without waiting for culture results given the risk of rapid deterioration in cirrhotic patients.

clinicalPearls: An ascitic-fluid PMN (neutrophil) count of at least 250/microL is diagnostic of SBP, irrespective of whether cultures grow an organism (Harrison 22e p.329, 372, 1070).

Fever is the single most common manifestation, present in roughly 80% of cases; abdominal pain, acute onset, and peritoneal signs aid diagnosis but their absence does not rule SBP out (Harrison 22e p.1070).
Abdominal tenderness is found in only about 40% of patients and rebound tenderness is uncommon, so a benign abdomen does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329).

SBP can present with no abdominal symptoms at all, instead manifesting as new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, altered mental status, jaundice, or acute kidney injury without another explanation (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715).

In any cirrhotic patient hospitalized with ascites who deteriorates or shows signs of infection, a diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory; tapping within 12 hours of admission lowers mortality through early SBP detection (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715).

Ascitic fluid should be injected directly into blood-culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield, and blood cultures drawn simultaneously, since the organism burden in the fluid is low and bacteremia frequently coexists (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).
Culture samples should be obtained before antibiotics are started to maximize recovery of the organism (Harrison 22e p.1070).
SBP is almost always monomicrobial; a single isolate is the rule (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).
Gram stain of ascitic fluid is frequently negative in SBP and a negative result should not deter treatment (Harrison 22e p.1070).
SBP virtually always arises on a background of preexisting ascites, which predates the infection (Harrison 22e p.1070).

A repeat paracentesis after 48 hours of therapy should confirm at least a 25% fall in the ascitic PMN count from baseline; failure to fall, or persistent ascitic leukocytosis after treatment, should prompt a search for an alternative or secondary diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071).
harrison.pathophysiology: SBP is spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid in the absence of an intraabdominal surgical source. The presumed mechanism is bacterial translocation: gut flora cross an edematous, leaky intestinal wall into mesenteric lymph nodes, producing bacteremia that seeds the ascites, which is a good growth medium. Susceptibility in cirrhosis reflects impaired hepatic filtration from a diseased liver and altered portal circulation, low ascitic complement levels (lower than in non-cirrhotic ascites), and diminished opsonic and phagocytic function of PMNs in advanced liver disease. Cirrhosis is also associated with gut dysbiosis (increased Enterobacteriaceae), small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, reduced Paneth-cell defensins, decreased intestinal motility, reduced pancreatobiliary secretions, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy, all of which promote pathologic translocation. SBP occurs in up to ~30% of hospitalized cirrhotics with ascites but is an uncommon event overall, affecting 10% or fewer of cirrhotic patients. (Harrison 22e p.1070, 2715)
additionalDifferentials: Secondary bacterial peritonitis from a perforated or inflamed viscus or intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071)
Hepatic encephalopathy from other precipitants (GI bleed, volume depletion, hyponatremia, constipation) when SBP presents as altered mentation (Harrison 22e p.2716-2717)
Acute kidney injury / hepatorenal syndrome from non-infectious causes when SBP presents as renal deterioration (Harrison 22e p.329, 2716)
infectionMimics: Secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforated viscus, ruptured appendix/diverticulum/ulcer, intraabdominal abscess) (Harrison 22e p.1071-1072)
Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax (Harrison 22e p.330)
Tuberculous peritonitis (ascitic lymphocytosis; can complicate or mimic infected ascites) (Harrison 22e p.373)
nonInfectiousMimics: Peritoneal carcinomatosis / malignant ascites (low-SAAG ascites; SBP is rare in malignant ascites) (Harrison 22e p.372-373)
Pancreatic ascites (high ascitic amylase, typically >1000) (Harrison 22e p.373)
Worsening uncomplicated tense ascites with increased girth but no infection (Harrison 22e p.329)
additionalInvestigations: Ascitic fluid PMN/neutrophil count (>=250/microL is diagnostic) (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070)
Ascitic fluid inoculated into blood-culture bottles at the bedside (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070)
Gram stain of ascitic fluid (often negative; does not exclude SBP) (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and ascitic total protein to characterize the underlying ascites and assess risk (Harrison 22e p.372)
Ascitic glucose and LDH when secondary peritonitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.373)
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to seek an intraabdominal source / exclude secondary peritonitis (Harrison 22e p.1070-1071)
Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air (perforation) when abdominal pain is present (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Repeat paracentesis at 48 hours to confirm >=25% fall in ascitic PMN count (Harrison 22e p.329)
redFlags: New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy or altered mental status in a cirrhotic with ascites (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715)
Unexplained acute kidney injury, jaundice, or nonlocalizing malaise/fatigue in a susceptible patient (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Multiple organisms recovered from ascitic fluid, especially with anaerobes, suggesting secondary peritonitis requiring source control (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071)
Free air under the diaphragm on imaging, signaling perforation (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Concurrent GI/variceal bleeding, which markedly increases SBP frequency (Harrison 22e p.330, 2716)
Failure of the ascitic PMN count to fall, or persistence of WBCs after therapy, indicating treatment failure or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071)
harrison.prognosis: SBP is a common and potentially lethal complication of cirrhotic ascites and carries significant morbidity and mortality, largely because it tends to occur in patients with the most advanced liver disease. In-hospital mortality is roughly 17-25%; one tertiary-center series reported ~23% mortality at 30 days and ~37% at 90 days. Recurrence is high, with up to ~70% of patients having another episode within a year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within about 72 hours. The underlying prognosis of cirrhosis with ascites is itself poor, with under 50% surviving 2 years after ascites onset in some series, so SBP should prompt consideration of liver transplantation. (Harrison 22e p.1071, 2715-2716, 373)
pitfalls: Diagnosis rests on the ascitic PMN count >=250/microL, not on a positive culture; ascitic cultures are often negative because the organism burden is low (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).

Recovery of more than one organism (a mixed flora, especially with anaerobes) alongside an elevated PMN count points to SECONDARY peritonitis from a ruptured viscus or abscess, not SBP, and demands a search for a surgical source (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071).
Multiple organisms WITHOUT an elevated PMN count suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle rather than true infection (Harrison 22e p.329).

Failing to perform a diagnostic paracentesis in a decompensated cirrhotic who deteriorates (encephalopathy, AKI, sepsis) misses SBP, since the abdomen may be benign and tenderness is present in only ~40% (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715).
A low ascitic total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL) reflects low opsonic activity and identifies patients at higher risk for SBP; this group warrants heightened suspicion (Harrison 22e p.330, 1071).

The 250/microL PMN threshold is specific to SBP and should not be applied to secondary peritonitis or to peritoneal-dialysis peritonitis, where lower leukocyte cutoffs are used (Harrison 22e p.1070, p.2486 context).
Gastric acid suppression (e.g., proton-pump inhibitors) has been associated with increased SBP risk in observational data (Harrison 22e p.1071).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system specific to SBP. Risk stratification is framed around predictors of poor outcome and renal injury: higher SBP risk in patients with low ascitic-fluid total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL), impaired renal function (creatinine >=1.2 mg/dL, BUN >=25 mg/dL, or serum sodium <=130 mEq/L), and advanced liver failure (Child-Turcotte-Pugh score >=9, bilirubin >=3 mg/dL); these are used to identify candidates for prophylaxis. The greatest benefit of adjunctive albumin is seen in those presenting with serum creatinine >=1 mg/dL, BUN >=30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >=5 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.1071)
